summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted Conversational API focusing on streaming responses, tuning generation params, and robust retry strategies for production usage. Discussed token costs, console observability, and enterprise controls (SSO, SOC2, VPC). Agreed next steps to run a lightweight benchmark and share security docs.
topics: console traces and token cost breakdown
transcript:
00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the account lead. Quick audio check?
00:06 Speaker 2 (Samir): Hi Maya yes, loud and clear.
00:09 Speaker 3 (Lena): All good here.
00:11 Speaker 1 (Maya): Awesome. Evan, do you want to say hi and what you'll cover?
00:15 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yeah hi, Evan Cho, Solutions Eng. I'll run the console demo — quick walkthrough of our hosted Conversational API, show streaming, typical params like temperature and max_tokens, and then drill into retry patterns and how to keep latency predictable with batching and cache.
00:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): Great, our team is mostly concerned about user-facing chat latency and cost per request, and we also have compliance questions.
00:36 Speaker 1 (Maya): Perfect, we'll cover that. Quick agenda: 1) live demo, 2) parameter tuning and tradeoffs, 3) retries/fallbacks and idempotency, 4) Q&A and next steps.
01:02 Speaker 4 (Evan): Alright share screen... okay starting on the Console. Here you can see model catalog — for chat we recommend the 7B quant variant for low-latency UIs, or the 13B when you need higher quality. Note: names might display differently in our UI, sometimes we show model nicknames.
01:30 Speaker 3 (Lena): Quick question, is that quantized model still good for retrieval-augmented generation?
01:34 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yes in many cases — quality drop is small for short answers; if you have long context or chain-of-thought we usually recommend the larger fp16 variant. Also you can pin a version.
01:48 Speaker 1 (Maya): Samir, can you remind us of your typical message lengths and concurrency?
01:52 Speaker 2 (Samir): Average prompt size is small, maybe 150 tokens, but sometimes we send 1.2k when we include product context. Peak concurrent users ~300, but requests are bursty — we see spikes to 1200 qps across services.
02:10 Speaker 4 (Evan): Good to know. So two knobs matter: batching (to control throughput/cost) and streaming (for UX latency). Our streaming path sends tokens as soon as they're generated — you can set chunk size and max latency per chunk.
02:28 Speaker 3 (Lena): Can you show how streaming looks on the SDK?
02:31 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yep. Here's a node snippet —
02:35 Speaker 4 (Evan): (reads) const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-7b-q', messages, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 256 }); stream.on('token', token => render(token));
02:52 Speaker 3 (Lena): Nice. And what about backpressure — if our frontend can't render that fast?
02:56 Speaker 4 (Evan): We have a client-side buffer and server-side pacing. You can request a smaller chunk_size and the server will pause between chunks; there's also a max inflight bytes setting. If the network is slow, you may see slightly higher latency, but no token loss.
03:15 Speaker 2 (Samir): Ok what about retries and duplicate outputs if we retry?
03:18 Speaker 4 (Evan): Great question. For idempotent behavior we recommend POST with a client-supplied idempotency_key. For streaming you can start the request with the key, and if you get a transient error (429, 503) use exponential backoff and then resume — the backend detects same key and can replay or return the cached response in many cases. If you need deterministic dedupe you can include a request hash.
03:41 Speaker 3 (Lena): Does the API return Retry-After on 429s?
03:44 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yes, we include Retry-After when it's available and also surfaced in our SDK as retryAfterMs. The default retry policy in our SDK is 3 attempts with jittered exponential backoff.
03:55 Speaker 1 (Maya): Also note for large spikes we support burst reservations for Dedicated customers but for Hosted we recommend graceful degradation patterns — degrade to a smaller model, or a cached canned response.
04:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): For SLOs we need tail latency under 400ms for <200 token responses — are those realistic on hosted?
04:19 Speaker 4 (Evan): For small responses and the 7B quant model yes in many regions you can get sub-300ms p50 and tail depends on batch behavior. We can run a short benchmark to validate against your real workload.
04:33 Speaker 3 (Lena): Yeah a benchmark would help. Also we care about token-level cost.
04:37 Speaker 4 (Evan): In the Console you'll see token-level breakdowns per route — request tokens vs response tokens and the cost estimate. We also expose a cost-per-token model and per-route attribution for customers.
04:51 Speaker 1 (Maya): Switching to params tradeoffs — temperature, top_p, repetition penalty, max_tokens. Evan can you show a quick A/B in the sandbox?
04:58 Speaker 4 (Evan): Sure — (types) sending same prompt with temp 0.0 vs 0.8. At 0.0 output is deterministic and concise; at 0.8 you get more creative but variance increases and sometimes you need extra safety checks. For shopping chat we usually see temp 0.2-0.4 is best.
05:25 Speaker 3 (Lena): Any guidance on stop sequences for multi-turn?
05:28 Speaker 4 (Evan): Use explicit stop tokens for the assistant turn boundaries, and if you rely on structured output use schema enforcement with our function-calling or a JSON schema postprocessor in the Console. That reduces parsing errors significantly.
05:47 Speaker 2 (Samir): Regarding security — we need SOC 2, SSO, and bring-your-own-key (KMS).
05:52 Speaker 4 (Evan): We support SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations for Private deployments; hosted customers can have envelope encryption and managed keys. We'll attach our SOC 2 summary.
06:04 Speaker 1 (Maya): Evan, can you demo a retry scenario?
06:07 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yep I'll simulate a 503. (types) triggering transient 503... you can see the client logs a transient error and the SDK retries with exponential backoff; after the third attempt it falls back to a cached reply per policy. In the Console you can trace retries and see events for each attempt in the request trace.
06:27 Speaker 3 (Lena): Is the fallback configurable?
06:29 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yes — per-route fallback policies: model fallback, cached response, or a static message. You can set max_attempts and whether to retry on 429s or only on 5xx.
06:42 Speaker 2 (Samir): For idempotency and at-least-once semantics, we can't accept duplicated charges. How is billing handled if a retry completes twice?
06:51 Speaker 4 (Evan): Billing is tied to final accepted response; duplicate attempts with same idempotency_key are reconciled so you don't get double-charged. We'll share the exact billing spec.
07:05 Speaker 3 (Lena): On observability, can we hook tracing to our existing APM?
07:09 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yes, we emit trace headers and you can instrument with OpenTelemetry. Console traces include request_id, attempt ids, model version, and token counts.
07:23 Speaker 1 (Maya): Quick note on Optimize: our Optimize tool suggests batching params and quantization profiles based on token distributions. Evan can show a saved suggestion later.
07:33 Speaker 4 (Evan): (switch) here's Optimize -> it suggests batch_size 8 for this workload and a prefix caching TTL of 30s which should reduce tokens by ~18% for similar prompts. Those are estimates until we run a real replay.
07:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): That could be big for cost.
07:52 Speaker 4 (Evan): Yup. Also, continuous batching can help but increases p95 latency; you can set latency SLOs and Optimize will recommend the right balance.
08:05 Speaker 3 (Lena): Ok what's a sensible pilot? We want to test basic chat for product recommendations for 5k monthly active users.
08:11 Speaker 1 (Maya): A lightweight pilot: 2-week benchmark with sample traffic replayed into hosted endpoints, collect latency, token-cost, and quality metrics. Evan runs benchmark, we share a report and suggested config.
08:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): Sounds good. Who owns the infra? We have strict VPC requirements for some data.
08:27 Speaker 4 (Evan): For VPC/private deployments we can self-host control plane or provide Private deployment — that typically takes longer. For pilot hosted is easiest; we can discuss a private lane if data residency is required.
08:45 Speaker 3 (Lena): One last thing — how are model rollouts handled to avoid regressions?
08:48 Speaker 4 (Evan): Rollouts are per-model-version with canary traffic, A/B testing, and automatic rollback on quality regressions tied to your evals. Console shows evaluation snapshots and alerting if metrics drop.
09:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): Okay wrapping up — quick recap and next steps. Maya to send security docs and pricing, Evan to run benchmark, Lena to share traffic profile.
09:16 Speaker 2 (Samir): Thanks everyone. Look forward to the benchmark.
09:19 Speaker 3 (Lena): Thanks.
09:20 Speaker 4 (Evan): Thanks team, I'll follow up with the SDK snippets.
09:23 Speaker 1 (Maya): Meeting end.
